bullets: How arithmetic progressions add d each step, geometric progressions multiply by r, and their sums build up term by term
slides.heading: JC H2 sequences: arithmetic and geometric progressions
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we build sequences from two moves only - adding the same difference again and again, and multiplying by the same ratio again and again - and by the end you will be able to write the nth term of each, add up their terms, and explain why u_10 takes nine jumps of d, not ten.

bullets: Write the nth term of an arithmetic progression, u_n = a + (n - 1)d, and of a geometric progression, u_n = a x r^(n - 1)
Find partial sums and sums to infinity - while remembering that the first term already sits at the start, before any jump
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things, including spotting the ten-jumps trap.

bullets: The terms 5, 8, 11, 14, ... climb by 3 every step, starting at 5
To reach the 10th term, how many jumps of 3 do you make - ten, or nine?
slides.heading: Ten terms, how many jumps?
slides.notes: Ask the class: the 10th term is ten terms along, so is it ten jumps from the start? Take two or three answers, then say: hold that thought, because counting the jumps honestly is the whole lesson in miniature.

bullets: An arithmetic progression adds the same common difference d every step: the jumps between terms are equal
A geometric progression multiplies by the same common ratio r every step: the jumps grow or shrink by that factor
A partial sum S_n adds the first n terms one by one; only a geometric progression with |r| < 1 has a sum to infinity
slides.heading: Two moves: add d, or multiply by r
slides.notes: Say this part slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: every sequence in this topic is built by repeating one of two moves, and every formula just counts how many times the move has been made.

bullets: Starting from 5 with d = 3, the marker hops the axis in equal jumps: 5, 8, 11, 14
The nth term counts the jumps made before it: u_n = a + (n - 1)d
slides.heading: Arithmetic progressions: add d each step
slides.notes: Point at the animation and narrate what is happening: watch the marker hop equal jumps - the first term sits at the start before any jump, so term number n has made exactly n - 1 jumps.

bullets: With r = 2 the terms 2, 4, 8, 16 double each step, and the jumps widen as the marker covers more ground
The nth term is the start multiplied once for each jump: u_n = a x r^(n - 1)
slides.heading: Geometric progressions: multiply by r each step
slides.notes: Watch the jumps double in size each time: multiplying by r is a move whose effect grows, because each new term is built from the whole of the term before it.

bullets: For 2, 4, 6, 8 the running total grows step by step: S_1 = 2, S_2 = 6, S_3 = 12, S_4 = 20
Pairing first and last terms gives the formula: S_n = (n/2)(a + l)
slides.heading: Seeing the sum build up
slides.notes: Watch each new term drop into the running total and the bar grow: the formula comes after the buildup, and pairing the first term with the last is what makes the shortcut honest.

bullets: With r = -1 the terms bounce 1, -1, 1, -1 forever - they never home in on one value
A sum to infinity exists only when the ratio shrinks the terms: |r| < 1, and then S = a / (1 - r)
slides.heading: A common mistake: r = -1 never settles
slides.notes: Watch the terms bounce between the same two values: bouncing is not settling, however close the two values sit. Convergence needs each jump to shrink the term, which is what |r| < 1 says.

bullets: Arithmetic: u_n = a + (n - 1)d - the a and d chips drop into place, with n - 1 counting the jumps
Geometric: u_n = a x r^(n - 1) - the same jump count appears as the power on r
slides.heading: The sequences toolkit
slides.notes: Two formulas, four moving parts: in both, the exponent or multiplier counts jumps, not terms - that single count is the toolkit, and it is exactly where the ten-jumps trap hides.

bullets: Step 1: a = 5 and d = 3, and u_10 sits nine jumps from the start, so u_10 = 5 + 9 x 3
Step 2: u_10 = 5 + 27 = 32 - not 35, because the first term is the start, not the first jump
slides.heading: Worked example: the 10th term of 5, 8, 11, 14, ...
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly and name the count as you write it; say: nine jumps, because the first jump lands on u_2 - counting jumps instead of terms is the move that keeps this formula honest.

bullets: Find u_6 of the geometric progression 3, 6, 12, 24, ... and state how many multiplications by r it took
Careful - a classmate writes: u_10 needs ten jumps of d, so u_n = u_1 + n*d. Explain to them why that is wrong, by counting where the first jump lands
slides.heading: Your turn: count the jumps, then correct
slides.notes: Give pairs two minutes, then cold-call one pair and press them on the trap: if the first jump lands on u_2, how many jumps has u_10 made?

bullets: Write the nth term of an arithmetic and a geometric progression, and find a partial sum
Explain why this claim is wrong: u_10 needs ten jumps of d, so u_n = u_1 + n*d.
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for the jump count in your last answer - if you can show u_10 = u_1 + 9d, you have cracked today's lesson.
